body:
## "This isn't about values, or aesthetics, or sentiment. In the end, a market is a business."

On April 1, in an office in the Gernas Building on Xinyuanli in Beijing, Zhang Qi and Bian Bian stood at a blackboard talking over a floor plan. It was a layout of the sunken plaza beneath the Sanlitun SOHO office towers, its indoor and outdoor space cut into zones marked A, B, C and D in big, hard-to-miss letters.

Two weeks later — today — a food market called Wude Chituoke opens in that plaza. Zhang Qi and Bian Bian are two of its founders. They graded the site by the way foot traffic moves through it, and charged different rents in different zones, to make sure every corner of the space earns its keep.

This is the fourth time Zhang Qi, Bian Bian and their third partner, Dai Kan, have run a food market in this sunken plaza. The event lasts three days, and this year the number of participating vendors rises to 91 — 20 more than at this point last year.

Zhang Qi thinks he is doing something fashionable. He named the market Wude Chituoke on purpose — a play on Woodstock, to borrow a little of its glow. Woodstock was the famous rock festival of 1969, named by *Rolling Stone* as one of the "50 Moments That Changed the History of Rock and Roll," and some people treat it as the defining event of young people at leisure and at play.

"We chase these labels. Labels raise awareness. But this isn't about values, or aesthetics, or sentiment," Zhang Qi says. "In the end, a market is a business."

Unlike department stores and shopping malls — traditional retail — the market is not yet a mature business.

In the days before a developed commodity economy, people met at a fixed spot to buy and sell goods: going to market. At those periodic markets you could shop, but you could also wander, eat, and watch jugglers. Today's markets have more professional operators and more ways to publicize themselves, but at bottom they still sell the same thing: a bundled shopping experience. Food markets salted with novelties are common all over the world. The most famous is the Brooklyn Night Bazaar in New York.

About two years ago, Zhang Qi told QDaily that he wanted to start a grassroots food market in Beijing — "a copy of the Brooklyn Night Bazaar."

Every weekend, hundreds of food obsessives, designers and artists gather in a 23,000-square-meter former factory in Greenpoint, Brooklyn. People taste food and watch performances; it is a mixed bag of everything. Live music counts for even more: bands rearrange their sets for the night market, building a cheerful soundtrack for the crowd. Like the juggling acts at markets of old, it works hard to pull people in and set a mood.

The vendors at the Brooklyn Night Bazaar know their business too. They write special menus for the night market and streamline how they get food out. No vendor sells more than two or three items, so it can serve a big crowd fast. Even large restaurants drop their per-item prices at the market: with 70 or 80 vendors in one space, the competition is naked, and a high price scares eaters off. Some vendors design packaging just for the market, so customers can keep it as a souvenir and eat as they walk.

What Zhang Qi pictured was a "low-frequency Brooklyn Night Bazaar." He would rent a lot in the middle of the city, only for a few days at a time, then pull together a few dozen small food vendors to sell on the spot, and make his money on tickets. If it went well, he could add live music and interactive pieces, and even sign up a few sponsors as deep pockets.

In 2015, Zhang Qi and his partners Bian Bian and Dai Kan ran three events on that plan. Tickets for the first one cost 30 yuan; 20,000 eaters turned up, and over three days they rang up 1 million yuan in sales. Zhang Qi was elated — he had found that a food market was a real business, and one that did not lose money out of the gate.

![Wude Chituoke's 2015 event](/uploads/image/201604/8d842d224948.jpg)

![](/uploads/image/201604/4b0e6a6424cd.jpg)

![](/uploads/image/201604/f2996300d596.jpg)

![](/uploads/image/201604/8474af1e806d.jpg)

![](/uploads/image/201604/161894dfec23.jpg)

![](/uploads/image/201604/7298f472e161.jpg)

![](/uploads/image/201604/a34a906422e9.jpg)

![Wude Chituoke's 2015 event](/uploads/image/201604/9fa54332bba8.jpg)

But much of it turned out to be harder than it looked.

Zhang Qi and Dai Kan soon found that running a food market works a little like running commercial real estate. To make the most money, think about location first. Then the number of well-known brands on site, the way foot traffic flows, sensible rents, how long visitors stay. Take a department store: different spots inside draw different numbers of customers. The ground-floor entrance is usually the easiest place to catch an eye, so prime ground like that goes to the counters that earn the most, cosmetics for instance. In a food market, stalls sit in different places and vendors run them with different skill, so three-day takings swing widely from one vendor to the next — anywhere from 4,000 to 40,000 yuan. They needed a zoning map of the site.

None of this was Zhang Qi's line of work. His earlier ventures had all been internet businesses. In 2009, he was still in media, editing a fashion and home-living channel. His first startup was a social network where users uploaded celebrity street-style photos and tagged the brands in them, but it was badly run and the site did not last. He then left media and went full time on Guowei Tiaopin, a site that funneled traffic to e-commerce platforms: editors picked out products you could buy and posted them, and whenever a customer bought one, Guowei Tiaopin split the sale with the platform. Guowei Tiaopin eventually stopped updating too. The trouble, Zhang Qi believes, was that "the barrier to entry in that industry was too low — we had no technical edge then, and it burned cash."

In 2014, in the middle of a conversation, Zhang Qi and Bian Bian hit on the idea of offline events. His first two startups had failed, but along the way he had met a lot of lifestyle brands. Bian Bian was then marketing director at the design e-commerce site Nuandao, and had run offline events herself. "From comic books to 3D and 4D movies to movie merchandise — in the end, people want to go to Disneyland. Sometimes people want to touch something," Bian Bian says. "Brands and products need a connection with users that has some warmth in it, and for that, a physical store can't be replaced."

An offline market is a physical store that exists on a whim. The first Wude Chituoke was held in March 2015, with 73 vendors, among them the independent ice cream brand Vivi Dolce, the tea brand Smash a Cup and the candy brand Sweetteeth — most of them brands the three founders knew from their previous jobs. In the end the small team put on three events in 2015, in spring, summer and winter, each on a different theme. Each drew a bigger crowd than the last, and by November a single event was doing 2 million yuan in sales.

Then the questions arrived. How do you keep the events going? And how often should you hold a food market like this?

All three founders, Zhang Qi included, had quit jobs to do this. If the events were too far apart, the income would not hold up. But they did not want to simply run more of them, believing that would flatten Wude Chituoke's growth as a brand. Young consumers, in other words, would soon find it stale.

There were other problems. Rents were rising, while ticket prices could not rise as fast. And most of the brands that came to the market were small, with no guarantee they would survive.

The Brooklyn Night Bazaar had been through all of this. On June 1 last year, its original site was leased to BMW, and rows of BMW SUVs replaced the noisy grassroots market. "BMW paid an extremely high rent, eight to ten times what we bid — a number we simply couldn't carry," said co-founder Belvy Klein. This summer they moved the Brooklyn Night Bazaar to Riis Park, but only as a stopgap: the beach is too far out, foot traffic is limited, and small vendors' earnings can't be guaranteed. Its founders are still hunting for the right space in the city, and will move the night market back the moment they can.

As Wude Chituoke's events grew, the costs — rent, building out the site, buying in content, live music, interactive pieces — squeezed Zhang Qi's team harder. They had to raise the ticket price, from 30 yuan in early 2015 to 50 yuan now, and they are talking to more sponsors. The one price that hasn't gone up is the vendor stall fee: last year it was 500 yuan for two days, and this year the cheapest is 700 yuan for three. Small vendors are the resource they most need to keep.

The market model seems to suit those small vendors. Independent brands usually price higher than the big brands sold everywhere, and they change their product lines slowly. An offline event works less as a way to lift sales than as a way to get known. "We have no expectations about revenue, we just think it's fun. Our prices on site are a bit lower than usual too — as long as people are happy. What matters is meeting a bunch of interesting brands. We've kept in touch with a lot of them, and it's led to chances to work together," says Tiepi, founder of Yongpu Coffee, a Shanghai brand started in 2011.

The market creates a mood for spending, but it also makes demands of small brands. They have to finish their products better, define what the brand stands for, know who they are selling to, actually make the thing well, and sell it through the right channels. A good-looking Taobao storefront is not enough.

Wude Chituoke now keeps in touch with more than 500 small food-and-beverage businesses, sorted into three tiers. The first is brands with finished products and the skill to run them, ranking in the top three of their niche — Jing-A, Traitor Zhou's popcorn, Saffron — and they have shops of their own. The second is independent brands, small and good. The third is interest groups. The first tier is about 20% of the total; the middle tier is the largest. Wude Chituoke set up an online sign-up form to take in new brands that are experimental, or built around an experience.

Foreign food-and-beverage brands make up 30% of the vendors at Wude Chituoke, and Chinese vendors have picked up how these foreign stallholders operate, bit by bit.

The founders of The Meatball Company are an American couple. They met Zhang Qi at a Beijing craft beer invitational festival. The two had put real work into their food packaging, and they joined last March's market. After that, The Meatball Company gradually became known, and later rented a narrow space on Dashibei Hutong by Shichahai, a stretch that also holds a cluster of hole-in-the-wall joints expats like.

Yongpu made a coffee for this year's market, using washed Ethiopian Yirgacheffe. "There's a floral, fruity aroma inside the acidity," Tiepi, Yongpu's founder, told QDaily. They have also worked with Xiaozaizi Theater on a new product to sell at the market.

The candy brand Sweetteeth made special tasting packaging for the market too, a marketing move: it will be handed out free to eaters who buy early-bird tickets. A game has been written into the plan for the first time as well — they are building a food treasure-hunt map with the food app Xiachufang. This is exactly the kind of operating know-how that Chinese independent food brands used to lack.

"We took part in other markets in Shanghai before, but there weren't many products like ours — mostly clothes or accessories — and the tone felt off, so we stopped considering them," Sweetteeth's founder told QDaily. As for takings at the market, they have no firm expectation. "Different vendors sell different things, at different costs and different prices. We sell candy, so if we can do 20,000 yuan over three days, that really is a well-run, mature market."

![The special tasting packaging Sweetteeth made for the market](/uploads/image/201604/67b7de345c91.jpg)

![Sweetteeth](/uploads/image/201604/eb6334ed7944.jpg)

![Yongpu tea bags](/uploads/image/201604/b70373a29e22.jpg)

![Yongpu coffee](/uploads/image/201604/9139df18e26b.jpg)

For now Wude Chituoke still runs on the three founders' own money. Zhang Qi rented an office a month ago, ending more than a year in which he, Bian Bian and Dai Kan worked wherever they could. "We finally have somewhere to sit. We can hire."

Investors have come to talk, one after another. Most of them want the food market to expand fast — 30 events a year, 10,000 people each, and you reach a trend-chasing crowd of 300,000. Beyond turning Wude Chituoke into a platform, they have floated other ideas: build a single payment system so small businesses can settle up on site, or rent one place as a permanent venue and make it an Airbnb for shops. Zhang Qi turned the money down. "We badly need exposure, but this isn't the time to think about harvesting." At this stage the team has to guarantee the quality of its products and its service; rushing to add more events does not look like a smart move.

They have, though, started taking part in commercial events in other cities. Early this year, a Wude Chituoke opened at Zhengzhou Dongrun City, a residential project in Baisha, Zhengdong New District, finished in May 2015. Forty-four vendors joined that Wude Chituoke, 11 of them brought in from Beijing and Shanghai by Zhang Qi's team, the rest recruited locally.

The vendors covered food, beer, accessories, clothing and crafts, and Zhang Qi put up two music stages. The developer believed this would pull a crowd into the mall quickly and lift the new project's profile. Out-of-town vendors were glad to use the event to test how their products played in another market. Zhang Qi's team recruited the vendors, staged the show and handled publicity. The developer absorbed the cost of the event, and paid the out-of-town vendors' travel as well.

In the market business, working with developers is nothing new. The Beijing Organic Farmers' Market started in 2006, holding an event every month or two at first; now it runs more than 150 a year. Besides picking sites near residential compounds, it also has long-term deals with shopping malls. "When we work with commercial landlords, the market usually doesn't pay a venue fee. The market brings foot traffic, so for the developer it's a win on both sides," Chang Tianle, who runs the Beijing Organic Farmers' Market, told QDaily.

![](/uploads/image/201604/79f43730dac2.jpg)

![](/uploads/image/201604/9e215e848797.jpg)

![](/uploads/image/201604/537e31c5e23d.jpg)

![](/uploads/image/201604/9a7ff2ae4ea8.jpg)

![Wude Chituoke's 2016 event in Zhengzhou](/uploads/image/201604/0c8ed09579d2.jpg)

This gave Wude Chituoke a second way to make money, on a model something like "win the name in the capital, win the profit outside it." This year they will plan more tightly and spread their revenue wider: six events, four in Beijing, one in Shanghai, one in another city. That puts Wude Chituoke in front of people once every two months.

"Build the name first. Harvesting the profit comes next," Zhang Qi says. He wants to create the next city brand that works the way a music festival does. Wude Chituoke still has some way to go.

Images courtesy of the Wude Chituoke markets in Beijing and Zhengzhou.
